1 Electrochemical insights into layered La2CuO4 perovskite: Active ionic copper for selective CO2 electroreduction at low overpotential Rana Pratap Singha,1, Payal Arorab,1, Subramanian Nellaiappanb,1, C.Shivakumarac, Silvia Irustad, Manas Paliwala, Sudhanshu Sharmab* aDepartment of Materials Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar, Palaj, Gandhinagar 382355, Gujarat, India bDepartment of Chemistry, Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar, Palaj, Gandhinagar 382355, Gujarat, India cSolid State and Structural Chemistry Unit, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore 560012, India dDepartment of Chemical Engineering and Environmental Technology, Nanoscience Institute of Aragon (INA), University of Zaragoza, 50018 Zaragoza, Spain Corresponding Author E-mail: ssharma@iitgn.ac.in (S.S). 1R.P.S, P.A. and S.N. have equally contributed to this work
2 Abstract La2CuO4, a layered perovskites oxide was synthesized using solution combustion method at different calcination temperatures. XRD characterization and Rietveld refinement analysis confirms the pure phase of the synthesized material. The effect of calcination causes shrinking in the lattice parameters affirm the change in the oxygen stoichiometry. Four Probe (Van der Pauw’s) and CP-AFM analysis were carried out to understand the influences of calcination temperature on electrical conductivity. Electrochemical investigations on La2CuO4 were performed at various negative potential ranges using cyclic voltammetry (CV) to identify the redox active centre. Thermodynamic calculations are further carried out to validate the electrochemical results in different mediums. Selective electrocatalytic conversion of CO2 to C2-hydrocarbon (C2H4) with FE% of 40.3% which is 10 times higher than CH4 (FE% = 4.1%) emphasized the in-situ formation of Cu2O from the redox active centre present in La2CuO4. Hydrocarbons are generated at a very low overvoltage (-0.4 V RHE) in comparison to literature. XPS analysis indeed confirms the presence of Cu+ species i.e., in-situ generated Cu2O, on La2CuO4 after CV and CO2 electrocatalysis. Keywords: La2CuO4; redox active centre; thermodynamics; CO2 electroreduction; C2hydrocarbon formation.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The structural features and property interplay of perovskites make them a unique material for diverse engineering applications. Generally, perovskites exists in various structural forms including oxide, organometallic, spinels and pyrochlores etc.[1] Among all the form, the layered perovskites are most significant. Lanthanum cuprate (La2CuO4) is a well-known stable layered perovskite oxide with K2NiF4 structure.[2-5] It consists of the perovskite layers with alternating rock-salt layers and it falls in orthorhombic perovskite category.[2, 4] La2CuO4 is made up of a perovskite ABO3 building block and a rock salt AO building block.[4] In regards to application, La2CuO4 has been reported as a catalyst for steam reforming of methanol [6], CO oxidation and NO abatement.[7] In addition, doped and undoped La2CuO4 is used as a photo catalyst for water splitting to generate H2.[8] La2CuO4 has also attracted a lot of attention as a superconducting material.[9-12] In previous studies, it is demonstrated that electrochemical oxidation can induce superconductivity in this material.[11, 12] Due to good electronic conductivity, electrochemical oxidation effectively converts La2CuO4 into superconducting La2CuO4+δ.[11] This conversion is reversible in electrochemistry and excess oxygen can be removed and added in the cyclic manner. Apart from the aforementioned study, a detailed investigation of electrochemical behaviour of La2CuO4, specifically in the negative potential range, is unavailable in literature. Whether the reduction cycle can generate oxygen defects and if these lattice defects are reversible or not, can only is ascertained by investigating detailed electrochemical behaviour of La2CuO4. With this aim, in the present work, electrochemistry and detailed conductivity studies on La2CuO4 have been investigated. In addition, thermodynamic calculations have been performed at different Eh and pH conditions to construct phase diagrams that demonstrate the possible electrochemical reactions during reduction and oxidation potentials. Reducibility of
4 the redox active centre ‘Cu2+’ in La2CuO4under different coordination environment is evaluated using a combined approach of electrochemistry and thermodynamic calculations. Further, the catalytic performance of La2CuO4 is evaluated by accelerating the redox active centre towards electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. In CO2 electroreduction, Cu is the only metal capable of converting CO2 into hydrocarbons and alcohols.[13-15] Especially its derived oxide form, i.e., formation of Cu2O from metallic Cu, is well known for the conversion of CO2 into C2-hydrocabons [16-23] due to the influences of Cu oxidation state. In this study, for the first time, in-situ formation of Cu2O from a layered La2CuO4 perovskite oxide is achieved and successfully utilized as catalyst for the selective electrocatalysis of CO2 to C2-hydrocarbon. Importantly, hydrocarbons are generated at -0.4 V RHE, a gain of about 500 mV compared to copper based catalysts reported in literature.

sections.heading: 2.1. Synthesis
sections.text:
La2CuO4 was synthesized by solution combustion method because this method is rapid and gives highly crystalline material.[24] Briefly, 5g of La(NO3)3.6H2O, 1.39 g of Cu (NO3)3.3H2O and 2.31g urea (NH2CONH2) were dissolved in 20-22 ml distilled water in a Pyrex dish. The solution was stirred using glass rod and the dish containing solution was introduced in a muffle furnace preheated at 300oC. The solution led to dehydration followed by combustion without any appearance of flame. Sample was ground in a mortar-pestle and calcined at 900oC for 10 hours to obtain the required polycrystalline sample. The synthesis reaction for the formation of La2CuO4 is given as: 2 La(NO3)3 + Cu(NO3)2 + 6.66 NH2CONH2  La2CuO4 + 10.66 N2 + 13.32 H2O + 6.66 CO2 ----- (1) Combustion synthesized La2CuO4 was characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) using Bruker D8 Discover diffractometer in the range of 20–80°. The Rietveld refinement was
5 performed using the FullProf-fp2k program varying different parameters simultaneously such as overall scale factor and background correction factor.

sections.heading: 2.2. Four-Probe Technique
sections.text: Conductivity measurements were performed with standard four-probe technique at room temperature. Sample pellets were made using die-set by applying constant pressure and resistance and measured using four-probe Van der Pauw’s method.[25] A constant current was passed through the two probes and the potential drop ‘V’ across the middle two probes was measured. The range of current was in between of 2μA and 2mA. Afterwards, conductivity of sample was determined using Ohm’s law.

sections.heading: 2.3. Conductive Probe- AFM
sections.text: CP-AFM studies were done with the instrument Bruker Nanoscope Multimode 8.0 using conducting probe. A 10mm diameter pellet of La2CuO4 was prepared to perform CP-AFM characterization. For sample preparation, metal plate was cleaned by acetone for removing dust or any other material. A small piece of carbon tape was put on the metal plate. Next, La2CuO4 pellet of about 2 mm of thickness and 10 mm of diameter was placed on the carbon tape of the metal plate. The edge of pellet was painted with the silver paste and dried for 2-3 minutes. Next, the metal plate containing sample compound is placed in CP-AFM instrument for AFM images.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical studies
sections.text:
Electrochemical studies were performed using the conventional three-electrode system using CHI-480E electrochemical workstation. All solutions were prepared using double-distilled water. Working electrode was made by mixing 100 mg of catalyst and 100 mg of 5% Nafion solution as binder. After that 600 μL of isopropanol was added to it to make thin slurry followed by deposition on a glassy carbon (GCE) electrode. The geometric area of the electrode was 0.071 cm2. Platinum wire was used as the counter electrode and Ag/AgCl
6 electrode was used as the reference electrode. NaHCO3 (0.5M) was used as the supporting electrolyte. Pure CO2 (99%) was purged in the cell setup to have proper solubility in electrolyte. An airtight electrochemical cell was used for the gaseous product formation and analysis. For quantification of gaseous products, a gas-tight syringe (Hamilton, 100μL) was used to transfer the evolved gases into a gas chromatograph (GC: CIC Baroda). Haysep-A column was used for separation and a Flame Ionization Detector (FID) for detection of CO and hydrocarbons. Thermal Conductivity Detector (TCD) was used for H2 detection. A standard gas mixture was used for calibrating the GC. For liquid products, Bruker 500 MHz Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectrometer is used. The Faradaic efficiency (FE %) is calculated based on the equation: ---- (2)FE% = n × F × N Q × 100 where, n is the number of electron transferred in the faradaic process; F is Faraday constant, 96485 C/mol; N is the amount of the generated product in this process; Q is the total charge passed through the whole reaction.

sections.heading: 2.5. Thermodynamic Modelling calculations
sections.text: The thermodynamic calculations for qualitative phase analysis of electrochemical reactions were performed using FactSage7.2 software (FThelgand FactPS databaseS) in aqueous medium.[26] The input parameter considerations to plot phase diagrams were taken as per the experimental conditions of the electrochemical reactions.[27]

sections.heading: 2.6. XPS analysis
sections.text:
The XPS was performed with Axis Ultra DLD 6 (Kratos Analytical Limited). The spectra were obtained by using the mono-chromatized AlKα source (1486.6 eV) run at 15 kV and 10 mA. For the individual peak regions, pass energy of 20 eV was used. Survey spectrum was measured at 160 eV pass energy. Analysis of the peaks was performed with the Casa XPS software, using a weighted sum of Lorentzian and Gaussian components curves after Shirley
7 background subtraction. The binding energies were referenced to the internal C (1s) (284.9 eV) standard.

sections.heading: 3.1. Characterization
sections.text:
X-ray diffraction patterns obtained for La2CuO4 synthesized using combustion technique and calcined at different temperatures is shown in Figure 1. XRD pattern of La2CuO4 powder calcined at 900oC matches well with the reported data in literature.[4] The calcination of the compound at 950°C for 10h improves the intensity suggesting the increase in the crystallinity (Figure 1b). XRD of sample calcined at 1000oC look similar to the sample calcined at 950oC and La2CuO4 phase is retained. The calcined sample at 1050oC shows some additional peaks, which enhance the noise in the XRD pattern. At 1100oC new peaks appear in the pattern indicating the presence of extra phase other than La2CuO4. These extra peaks are related to La2O2CO3, CuO, Cu2O and Cu [28-30]. Formation of La2O2CO3 is quite unexpected because this phase is usually not stable at this temperature. It is speculated that at high temperature, atmospheric CO2 is able to react with lanthanum species in La2CuO4 to form La2O2CO3. Calcination process in the temperature range of 900oC to 1000oC also causes shifting of the peak position as seen in Figure 2(a). In order to get the correct values of peak shifting; NaCl was added as the internal reference. Figure 2(a) shows shifting of highest intensity peak towards the higher 2θ value suggesting the shrink in the lattice up to 1000oC and beyond this temperature, the lattice expands to the original size. At 1000oC, it is expected that La2CuO4 contains excess oxygen due to the oxygen intercalation to form La2CuO4+δ showing a decrease in the lattice parameter.[9-12] As stated earlier, above 1000oC, La2O2CO3 phase along with CuO is formed and the excess oxygen is probably utilized in the formation of these compounds causing the lattice to expand again. Further, Rietveld refinement was carried out to investigate the effect of calcination temperature on lattice parameters and cell
8 volume of La2CuO4 at 900oC (Figure 2(b)) and 1000oC (Figure 2(c)). The estimated refined lattice parameters and cell volume is tabulated in Table 1. Low values of R factors demonstrate that the refinement is satisfactory. It is observed that as calcination temperature increases from 900 to 1000oC the refined lattice parameters (a, c) and their corresponding cell volume (v) decreases from (a = 5.3593 Å, c = 13.1573 Å, v = 381.04 Å) to (a = 5.3577 Å, c = 13.1536 Å, v = 380.76 Å). This might be due to the intercalation of oxygen molecules, as La2CuO4+δ contain excess oxygen that may shrink the lattice at high calcination temperature (1000oC). Evaluating the electrical conductivity of La2CuO4 is important to understand the electrochemical properties. Four-probe technique usually gives an idea about the electronic conductivity range and identifies the material which lies in semi-conducting to conducting range. Generally, electrical conductivity of solids is strongly dependent on temperature at which calcination is performed. Four-probe experiment shows that layered perovskites, La2CuO4 is generally electronically conducting in the temperature range 900-1100oC. The trend between conductivity (Ω-1m-1) and calcination temperature (oC) is shown in Figure 2(d). This figure indicates that conductivity rises to a maximum value and then decreases. Briefly, conductivity starts increasing from 950oC reaching a maximum value of 1.47 Ω-1m-1 at 1000oC. This is followed by a rapid reduction in conductivity at 1050oC. Conductivity further decreases at 1100oC giving the value of 0.15 Ω-1m-1. Decrease in the conductivity above 1000 oC is due to the formation of impure phases and dissociation of the lattice. Additionally, there have been various models proposed for aforementioned phenomenon.[31, 32] Result demonstrated in the 4-probe method can be confirmed further by conductiveprobe AFM study. The results of CP-AFM studies of two samples of La2CuO4 calcined at 900oC and 1000oC are shown in Figure 2(e-h). Simultaneous topography and current mapping images captured from 10 mm diameter pellet surfaces for the two samples as a
9 function of calcination temperature and at 0.025 V bias are shown in Figures 2(e,f) and 2(g,h), respectively. 3D images show that the compound calcined at 900oC has different grain size and it can be ascertained from tuna image that conductivity is not properly channelized (Figure 2(e,f)). Some points, i.e., grains on the surface of compound are conducting and conductivity is found on selective grains of the compound.[33] Grain size and density appears small in the La2CuO4 calcined at 900oC but appears comparatively larger in sample calcined at 1000oC (Figure 2(g,h)). Qualitatively, the number of conductive regions (as denoted by brighter areas) in the tuna image and overall surface conductivity (as denoted by an increase in the intensity of the brighter areas along with their numbers) are found to increase with increasing calcination temperature to 1000oC. These results further support the observation presented in four-probe conductivity measurement.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical studies on La2CuO4
sections.text:
Electrochemical behaviour of La2CuO4 calcined at 1000oC sample is studied by cyclic voltammetry (CV). Figure 3 show the continuous CV responses of La2CuO4 modified glassy carbon electrode at different potential ranges in 0.5 M NaHCO3 (pH 8) solution at 40 mV s-1 scan rate. CV in the range of 0.0 to -1.0 V (Figure 3(a)) shows a clear peak near to -0.17 V and one broad hump in the oxidation scan. In the subsequent scan, the reduction peak becomes clearer. In the range of 0.0 to -1.2 V three peaks in reduction scan at and one broad peak in oxidation scan is noticed (Figure 3(b)). The peak voltages in the reduction scan are - 0.16 V, -0.50 V and -0.93 V while the peak voltage in the oxidation scan is difficult to locate due to the broadness. Some of these peaks become sharper in the subsequent scan. The redox reactions are best visible when the potential range is changed to 0.0 to -1.4 V (Figure 3(c)) as the peaks are sharpest and clearly identifiable compared to previous graph. The oxidation peak is also quite clear with the peak voltage of -0.13 V (Figure 3(c)). Peak at -0.93 V, which appeared earlier (see Figure 3(b)) is not visible in this potential range probably due to
10
masking by the hydrogen evolution reaction. It is anticipated that all these redox peaks are
related to copper which is the only reducible species in La2CuO4. In Figure 3(c), first reduction peak at -0.16 V is due to Cu2+ to Cu+ reduction. Second reduction peak at -0.50 V is due to Cu+ to Cu0 (metal) reduction. Oxidation peak at -0.13 V is related to Cu (0) converting back to Cu2+[34.35]. Once the copper is reduced from Cu2+ to Cu+, it possibly comes out of
the La2CuO4 lattice generating La2O3 and Cu2O. This separated copper oxide then further reduces to Cu metal and works as the catalyst to give hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at -
1.2 V. In the oxidation scan this separated copper metal oxidizes to form CuO depicting a
peak at -0.13 V. Following are the reactions, which occur during a complete CV scan of
La2CuO4:
2 La2Cu (II)O4 + 2e-→ 2 La2O3 + Cu2(I)O + ½ O2 ---- (3) Cu2(I)O+ e-→ Cu0+ ½ O2 ---- (4) Cu0→ Cu2++ 2e- ---- (5)
Clearly, first two reactions are combination of electrochemical and chemical reactions where
oxidation state of copper changes from 2  1 0; accompanying the removal of lattice
oxygen. The last one is pure electrochemical reaction. Thus, the redox chemistry of active
centre on La2CuO4 is explored due to the interplay of lattice oxygen and the electron transfer. The reason for reduction peak appearing at -0.93 V is not known at this stage.
Clearly, La2CuO4 exhibits a complex redox behaviour that can be influenced by
surface activity of Cu and certainly by the position of La and Cu atoms in the crystal structure
of La2CuO4. The influence of redox active centre behaviour of copper on the La2CuO4 is ascertained by investigating the CV of copper metal strip (Figure 3(d)) in the potential range
of 0.0 to -1.3 V. As can be seen that the two step reduction and one step oxidation in Cu
metal is similar to La2CuO4 (Figure 3(c)). Third reduction peak at -0.9 V is also similar to La2CuO4 in Figure 3(b). As stated earlier the reason for this peak is unknown at this stage.
11
These observations indicate the similarity in the electrochemistry of both the compounds. The
peak voltages in the case of Cu metal are -0.12 V for oxidation and -0.16 V and -0.6 V for
reduction which are quite close to La2CuO4. In order to gain more insight into the redox behaviour of copper in solid phase, CV of pure CuO was conducted. In this compound,
copper is in the same +2oxidation state as in La2CuO4. Therefore, it will be a relevant model to compare the redox electrochemistry. The CV of CuO is shown in Figure 3(e). Oxidation
peaks appear approximately at -0.085 V and 0.07 V whereas reduction peak is seen at -0.26 V
depicting two step oxidation and one step reduction. This is in stark contrast to La2CuO4. Origin of the second oxidation peak at -0.09 Vis quite intriguing and it is speculated to be the
further oxidation of CuO to form hydroxide a common possibility in basic medium. CV of
La2CuO4 in the positive potential range (0.0 to 1.2 V) is shown in Figure 3(f) and it looks featureless with no indication of any redox reaction. The rise in current beyond 1.0 V may be
due to the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). The current at 1.2 V decreases in the successive
cycles confirming irreversible changes on the surface of the catalyst. It is evident that redox
behaviour of Cu and La2CuO4 is very similar depicting the similar redox chemistry in the negative voltage scans. On the other hand, the CV response of CuO was distinctly different
compared to La2CuO4 and Cu which confirms the formation of CuO is quite low during CV.
The electron transfer property of La2CuO4 is studied by varying the scan rates from 10
to 90 mVs-1 in 0.5 M NaHCO3 electrolyte solution (Figure 4(a)). While increasing scan rates (v), the respective anodic oxidation peak (ipa) and cathodic peak (ipc) currents at corresponding redox peak are increased with slight shift in Ep. A linear plot of peak current (ip) versus square root of the scan rate (v1/2) is drawn (Figure 4(b). The nature of this linearity is directly related to the higher conductivity of La2CuO4. Slight shift is also noticed in the peak voltages upon increasing the scan rate indicating the pseudo reversibility on the system.
12
In order to assist the understanding of the CV behaviour of these materials,
thermodynamic calculations were performed using FactSage [26] and the results are
presented in Figure 5. The calculations are performed at varying partial pressure of O2 and varying concentration of La2CuO4, CuO and Cu in 0.5 molar solution of NaHCO3. As seen in Figure 5, Iso-Eh and pH lines are superimposed along with the phase stability regions. The
arrows in Figure 5, represents the change in phase stability areas with respect to decreasing
Eh around 1 mole of La2CuO4, CuO and Cu. The calculation for La2CuO4 suggests (Figure 5(a)) the decomposition of La2CuO4 into Cu(OH)2 and La2O3 (region 4) in Figure 5(a) at the start of the CV experiment. With further application of reduction potential the Cu(OH)2 transforms to Cu2O in the Eh (electrode potential) range between -0.2 and -0.4 V. As the reduction potential is decreased beyond -0.4 V the calculation indicates the reduction of Cu2O into pure Cu in the Eh range between -0.4 and -0.8 V. On further lowering the potential, gas
evolution in presence of Cu is predicted by thermodynamic calculations. In general, the
calculations are in qualitative agreement with the experimental CV data of La2CuO4. The electrochemical behaviour at peak reduction voltages during the CV scan are reasonably
predicted by thermodynamic calculation. The only difference is the formation of Cu(OH)2 which is not noticed in the experimental results. In spite of this, fundamental behaviour of
La2CuO4 is same both in experiments and in calculations.
The calculation for pure Cu in 0.5 M NaHCO3 is shown in Figure 5(b). The results
indicate that at the start of the CV test, Cu oxidises to form mixed Cu(OH)2 and Cu2O (region 3 in Figure 5(b). As reduction potential is decreased, Cu2O is reduced to pure Cu in the potential range of 0.0 to -0.6 V. The further reduction in potential is marked by evolution of
gases as seen in region 6 in Figure 5(b). The experimental CV of pure Cu displays sharp
reduction peak at -0.16 V and -0.60 V. Reduction CV of La2CuO4 exhibits the same behaviour with the peak reduction voltages lying close to that of pure Cu. In case of La2CuO4
13
thermodynamic calculations reasonably predicted the reduction behaviour as Cu(OH)2 reduces to Cu2O followed by reduction to pure Cu. The CV range for the aforementioned reduction events were well predicted by the calculations as well. Thermodynamically
predicted electrochemical behaviour of CuO in presence of 0.5 NaHCO3 is shown in Figure 5(c). The calculations indicate that CuO is reduced to Cu2O at the start of the CV cycle followed by the reduction of Cu2O into pure Cu in the range of 0.0 to -0.4 V. This is agreement with the experimental peak reduction voltage at -0.2 V. The oxidation step of CV
scan indicates a peak voltage at -0.1 V which corresponds to formation of Cu2O (region 4 in Figure 5(c)), the second oxidation peak at 0.05 V, most probably indicates the formation of
Cu(OH)2 as indicated in region 2 of Figure 5(c). Using the experiments and the calculations, the reactions can be written as follows:
Cu2(I)O + e-→Cu + ½ O2 ----- (6) 2Cu0+ ½ O2→ Cu2(I)O+2e- ----- (7) Cu2(I)O → Cu(II)(OH)2 +e- ----- (8)
Formation of Cu2O from CuO is unnoticed in CV (Figure 3(e)) probably because it forms near 0.0 V right at the beginning of the CV. Therefore, CV represents the electrochemistry
after Cu2O is generated from CuO. This is the reason why only one reduction peak is noticed in the CV of CuO (Figure 3(e)). Two step oxidation processes in CuO is also different from
La2CuO4 and Cu. Thermodynamic calculations support this experimental observation as indicated in region 4 of Figure 5(a). Clearly, Cu(OH)2 is thermodynamically more stable than pure Cu in 0.5 M NaHCO3 solution for the Eh and pH range studied in this work.
The thermodynamic simulation of the electrochemical behaviour of La2CuO4, CuO
and Cu is dependent on the Gibbs energies (as a function of Eh and pH) of these compounds
along with compounds such as Cu2O, Cu(OH)2, La2O3 and different ionic species in aqueous phase. Along with the thermodynamic considerations, kinetic parameters such as surface
14
effect and coordination environment can account for the difference observed in the
electrochemical behaviour of La2CuO4 and CuO. For instance, in the former, Cu reduces in two steps destroying the crystal structure and in the later one reduction occurs in a single
step. This is probably due to the different coordination environment of the two compounds.
Cu in La2CuO4 (orthorhombic) is in octahedral environment with two long and six short bonds environment while in CuO (monoclinic) it is four coordinated in the square planer
geometry. This possibly affects the energetics of the redox reaction resulting into the different
electrochemical behaviour.

sections.heading: 3.3. Electroreduction of CO2
sections.text:
To examine the catalytic activity of La2CuO4 for CO2 electroreduction, CV
experiments were carried out in the N2 (blank) and CO2 saturated 0.5 M NaHCO3 (pH 8) electrolyte at 20 mV s-1 in the potential range of 0.0 to -1.2 V (Figure 6(a)). Gases are purged
for 30 minutes in the electrolyte solution prior to the experiments. In presence of CO2, enhanced cathodic current responses starting at an onset potential of about -0.2 V is observed. Cathodic current densities at -0.8 V, -1 V and -1.15 V are 0.9 mA cm-2, 1.2 mA cm-2 and 1.5 mA cm-2, respectively. The observed current density values are quite higher than the current densities in N2 saturated electrolyte. The values are 0.5, 0.54, 0.65 mA cm-2 at -0.80, -1.0 and -1.15 V (in blank). This observation confirms the electrocatalysis of CO2 occurred on La2CuO4 catalyst. Likely, the same experiment was repeated on CuO (Cu2+) for comparison (Figure 6(b)). CV of CuO is not stable beyond -0.8 V due to the influence of hydrogen
evolution reaction even in blank (N2) purged electrolyte. Enhancement in the cathodic current in CO2 saturated electrolyte up to -0.8 V is due to the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. As observed, HER is overtaken beyond -0.8 V which make the system unfavourable for CO2 electrocatalysis.
15
Further, steady state current responses (chronoamperometry) on La2CuO4 and CuO in
CO2 saturated electrolyte at -1.0 V vs. Ag/AgCl (i.e., -0.4 V RHE) is shown in Figure 6(c&d). The steady state current density is 0.5 mA cm-2 on La2CuO4 which is obtained in about 180 seconds and further the current density is maintained (Figure 6c). For CuO, the obtained current density is 0.29 mA cm-2, which is quite noisy and looks disturbed because of
HER is predominantly occurred at -1.0 V (Figure 6d), as seen in CV. In order to analyse the
products formed as a result of CO2 reduction after the chronoamperometry experiment mentioned above, the evolved gases were collected and subjected to gas chromatography.
The major gaseous products are CO, CH4, C2H4 and H2. Respective FID and TCD gas chromatograms are shown as inset of Figure 6(c&d). Additionally, liquid sample was also
collected after 2 hrs of electrolysis (in continuous CO2 bubbling), and subjected to NMR analysis. No liquid products could be detected probably due to very low yield and low
applied voltage. This is also depicted in terms of Faradaic efficiencies (FE %), estimated at -
1.0 V (Figure 6(e&f)). Calculated FE% of CO was very less than ~1 % onLa2CuO4 catalyst. Comparatively, the formation of C2H4 (C2-hydrocarbon) predominantly occurs more than CH4 (C1-hydrocarbon) on La2CuO4 catalyst. FE% of C2H4 is 40.3%, CH4 is 4.1 % and hydrogen is 29.1 % (at -1.0 V). It is interesting to note that the formation of C2H4 is 10 times more than CH4, which highlights the catalytic activities of La2CuO4. The observed C2H4/CH4 is ratio is comparable with the reported Cu2O electrocatalyst (Table 2), confirming the in-situ formation of Cu2O from La2CuO4. Likewise, on CuO, FE% of CO is <1%, CH4 is 25.5 %, C2H4 is 9.8%, and hydrogen is 35.5 % (at -1.0 V vs. Ag/AgCl). It is evident that CH4 is more than C2H4 in the case of CuO (ratio of C2H4: CH4 = ~0.4), which is in stark contrast to La2CuO4. This observation reconfirms the in-situ formation of Cu2O species responsible for enhancing the selectivity and faradaic efficiencies of C2H4 [16-19,23]. It is extremely important to note that the hydrocarbons are being generated at -1.0 V which is -0.4 V RHE
16
about 500 mV lesser than the best performing catalyst in Table 2. This clearly indicates that
the ionic Cu in La2CuO4 is able to produce significant hydrocarbons at such a low over potential.
In order to confirm the in situ formation of Cu2O from La2CuO4, high resolution XPS
analysis is performed for as-prepared La2CuO4 as well as after electrochemical treatment (Figure 7). As can be seen, deconvoluted XPS of Cu-2p3/2 spectra of pure La2CuO4 showed two distinct peaks at binding energy (B.E.) of 934.5 eV and 943.7 eV respectively (Figure
7(a)).[36,37] Peak at 934.5 eV represents the +2 oxidation state of Cu species along with strong satellite peak at 943.7 eV. This infers the presence of native ionic Cu2+ species in
La2CuO4. In case of La2CuO4 after CV, a new peak is appeared at lower B.E. of 932.5 eV which is correspond to Cu+ species. This is accompanied with diminishing of satellite peak at 943.7 eV confirming the reduction of Cu2+ (Figure 7(b)) and formation of stable Cu2O [37]. This reaction is also identified in the CV behaviour of La2CuO4. Peak at 932.5 eV of Cu+ is retained even after the steady state chronoamperometry experiment in CO2 saturated solution (Figure 7(c)), further confirming the stable Cu+ formation. From this observation, we can
conclude that the in situ formation of stable Cu2O in La2CuO4 after during CV and CO2 electroreduction. This Cu+ is responsible for high ethylene selectivity.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
Combustion technique is an excellent method to prepare layered La2CuO4 perovskites.
XRD analysis confirmed the high purity and crystalline nature of the synthesized La2CuO4 catalyst. Four-probe and AFM studies reveal that conductivity first increases then decreases
as per the calcination temperature. Increase in the conductivity can be attributed to the lattice shrink due to excess oxygen insertion that occurs at 1000oC which was later confirmed
through Rietveld refinement analysis. On the other hand, decrease in the conductivity at >1000oC is due to the formation of impure phases such as La2O2CO3, CuO, Cu2O and Cu.
17
Electrochemical behaviour of the calcined compound shows that La2CuO4 is unstable in the negative potential range and dissociates into La2O3 and Cu2O. This Cu2O further undergo reduction to form Cu metal at more negative voltage than -0.50 V. This is confirmed by
investigating the CV behaviour of Cu metal strip where both Cu metal and La2CuO4 depict similar redox chemistry including two step reduction and single step oxidation.
Thermodynamic calculations aided in understanding and verifying the electrochemical
reactions associated during the CV measurements of La2CuO4, CuO and Cu. The calculations reasonably predicted the experimentally observed reduction and oxidation peaks and assisted
in understanding the electrochemical behaviour of these solid compounds. Selective
electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to C2-hydrocarbon (10 times higher than CH4) demonstrates the in-situ formation of Cu2O from La2CuO4 during the CO2 electroreduction reaction. Importantly, these hydrocarbons form at -0.4 V RHE, very low overpotential compared other reported copper based compounds. XPS analysis confirms the presence of Cu+ species (i.e.,
Cu2O) after electrochemical treatment of La2CuO4 and retained after selective CO2 electrocatalysis.
